The red light pulsed steadily above my headset, a small, insistent heartbeat in the otherwise quiet room. It was 3:17 AM, a notoriously slow shift at the Crisis Response Center. Most calls were variations on “I’m feeling hopeless,” or “I don’t see a point,” a familiar tapestry of despair woven by countless voices before me. I’d developed a kind of numb empathy, a ability to recognize the tremor of desperation beneath the words, to offer a calm presence without getting completely swallowed by the darkness.

“Hello?” I asked, my voice carefully neutral, projecting warmth without sounding like a practiced reassurance. “This is Sarah, Crisis Response. Can you tell me what’s going on?”

The voice was hesitant, choked with something that sounded like static. “I… I don’t know if this is right. I don’t know if anyone can help.”

That was standard. “You’re safe right now,” I said, following protocol. “Just talking about it can be a first step. Can you tell me a little about what’s making you feel this way?”

The silence stretched, punctuated only by the hum of the server room. Then, a small, broken sob. “I just… I feel like I’m drowning. Everything is just… too much.”

I guided them through the standard questions, gently probing for details, acknowledging their pain. They spoke of work, a demanding boss, a string of recent failures, a overwhelming loneliness that clung to them like a shadow. I offered coping mechanisms – deep breathing, grounding techniques, lists of resources. I stayed on the line for forty-five minutes, diligently adhering to the guidelines, trying to make a tangible difference, however small. 

Finally, they said, “Thank you. Really. I… I think I need to go to bed.” 

“Of course,” I replied, preparing to log the call as ‘low risk, verbal support provided.’ “Just remember, you can call us back anytime, day or night.

The rustling was… underwhelming. I’d expected a veritable tidal wave of flesh-bound horrors, a black tide consuming everything. Instead, there were a *lot* of rustles, a consistent, slightly mournful shuffle through the debris-strewn streets of what was once Denver. Zombies. A glut of them. And, depressingly, they seemed mostly interested in furniture.

Being a Lich in the 21st century was profoundly disappointing. The grand, apocalyptic prophecies, the inevitable subjugation of humanity, the sweeping, dramatic reign of undeath – all of it felt rather…muted. The zombies were just…there. A persistent, low-grade inconvenience. Like an overly enthusiastic, perpetually hungry roommate.

My name is Xantus, and I’ve been dead for approximately 742 years. I’ve overseen empires rise and fall, mastered arcane arts beyond the comprehension of modern scholars, and debated philosophy with beings of unimaginable power. And now, I was primarily concerned with securing a decent supply of desiccated beef jerky.

The problem was, nobody took a seven-hundred-year-old skeleton seriously. Or, more accurately, they didn't *believe* they were a seven-hundred-year-old skeleton. Most people saw a unusually well-preserved, if somewhat grumpy, old man in a very formal, very impractical suit. The suit was, admittedly, a boon. The flowing black robes of my former era were a logistical nightmare in a world dominated by collapsed infrastructure and rampant chaos. Plus, the tailored cut was excellent for maintaining a semblance of dignity.

“Excuse me,” I’d say, attempting a commanding tone, “I require assistance. I need to reinforce the warding runes on my perimeter.”

They’d either recoil in terror, scream, or, most commonly, politely suggest I contact the National Guard. The National Guard was, predictably, not equipped to deal with a Lich. They mostly dealt with… zombies. A rather frustrating overlap.

The rain was the color of weak tea, blurring the edges of everything. I was standing on a sidewalk in a neighborhood I didn’t recognize, a place that looked like it had been meticulously assembled from the most unremarkable parts of several American suburbs. Beige houses, manicured lawns, identical mailboxes—the whole aesthetic screamed “comfortable conformity,” and I was desperately uncomfortable. I’d been wandering for hours, lost in a fugue state after…well, after *it*.

“It” was a notebook. A small, unassuming black notebook with a plain, silver clasp. And “it” was capable of ending lives.

I'd found it tucked behind a dumpster in a alleyway near my apartment, a place I’d usually avoid. It was a blatant rip-off of the infamous Death Note, just…less. Significantly less. Instead of the hauntingly elegant script of the original, the writing on the pages was a slightly shaky, easily legible block font. Instead of the soul-crushing despair of writing a name and watching someone vanish, this thing only produced minor annoyances.

At first, I’d been skeptical. I’d tested it, of course, out of morbid curiosity. I’d written "Mr. Johnson, the guy who always parks in my spot," and the next morning, his meticulously waxed car was covered in a generous coating of bird droppings. Then, I’d written "The barista at Starbucks who always misspells my name," and he’d started consistently adding an extra shot of espresso to every drink, resulting in a mildly frantic, jittery customer base. 

It was… pathetic. Utterly, unbelievably pathetic. I’d almost put the notebook back in the dumpster when I’d seen a small, handwritten note tucked inside the front cover.

“Welcome to the family. You’ve inherited the Mild Inconvenience Note.”

The fluorescent lights of the Tribunal felt colder than they had any right to be. They hummed with a unsettling neutrality, a stark contrast to the swirling chaos of my thoughts. I sat rigidly in the obsidian chair, the smooth surface digging into the back of my thighs, a uncomfortable reminder of my current predicament. I was dead. Or, at least, awaiting judgment. And I’d done something monumentally, ridiculously, *wrong*. I’d hired Satan as my attorney.

The process was… baffling. When you die, you’re taken to this neutral space, stripped of all earthly possessions and identities beyond your core essence – your memories, regrets, and the general sum of your being. Then, a tribunal of impeccably neutral-faced beings, all shades of grey and vaguely reminiscent of librarians, informed you of your rights, the most important of which was the right to legal representation.

Everyone, it seemed, was choosing. Lawyers specializing in the afterlife – celestial advocates, demons of defense, and even a surprisingly competent spirit lawyer who'd previously defended a particularly pious merchant – were in high demand. I was different. I’d chosen… him.

Satan.

The audacity had been intoxicating, fuelled by a lifelong fascination with the dramatic and a desperate, illogical need to be the first. The application process was simple, requiring only a written statement of intent. I’d drafted a passionate plea, arguing that my life had been filled with morally gray choices, a constant dance between good and bad, and that a truly just assessment required someone who understood the complexity of the human heart – a heart, frankly, capable of profound darkness.

And to my utter shock, he’d accepted.

Now, here I was, facing the tribunal, a nervous sweat clinging to my forehead, waiting for my… advocate. The lead librarian-like figure, a woman named Ms. Eklund, cleared her throat. “The representative for the defendant, Mr. John Smith, is present.”

The rain in Havenwood was a permanent fixture, a greasy, insistent blanket clinging to the perpetually overcast sky. It smelled of rust and something vaguely organic – decaying leaves, probably, or something less pleasant. Havenwood wasn't a place you *went* to; it was a place you ended up, usually after making a bad decision. And I, formerly known as Bluebell, was currently nestled in a doorway on Maple Street, nursing a bruised rib and a burgeoning headache.

Bluebell wasn’t a fairy. Not anymore. Not really. The shimmer was gone, the wings long since traded for a well-worn leather jacket, a scavenged utility belt, and a permanent squint from staring at the bleak landscape. The “Havenwood Fairy Council” was a myth, a quaint legend whispered by the desperate, a bureaucratic nightmare that had ultimately dissolved into corruption and, eventually, complete and utter collapse. 

I was a problem solver. That’s what the… the *clients* called me. Mostly, I solved problems that the police wouldn't touch, or couldn’t understand. Missing pets with a suspicious bite mark. Vanished children who weren't exactly volunteers. The occasional adult who’d stumbled too far into the woods and forgotten how to find their way back. I operated on the fringes, a ghost in a town built on secrets.

My payment was rarely money. Usually, it was information, a small favor, or sometimes, a bottle of whiskey strong enough to strip paint. Tonight, it was a crumpled photograph of a girl – seven or eight, with bright, terrified eyes – and a desperate plea from her mother: “Find her. Please.” 

The girl was named Lily. And Lily had vanished from the annual Havenwood Harvest Festival, a nauseating display of forced cheerfulness held every year to appease the… *residents*. The air in the hall was thick with anticipation, a strange blend of perfume, apprehension, and something subtly metallic – the scent of ritual. Hundreds of women, clad in obsidian gowns embroidered with silver filigree, sat in perfect, silent rows. Each was a pillar of a different, ostensibly independent organization: a financier, a diplomat, a philanthropist, a tech mogul, a journalist – all outwardly involved in discreet global influence, but all, undeniably, connected to the same, invisible thread. Tonight was the Convergence, the night the Silent Order, known only as “The Weavers,” unveiled their Master Plan.

For centuries, they had operated in the shadows, subtly nudging humanity along a carefully considered path. The Illuminati, the Freemasons, the Bilderberg Group – they were merely branches on a far grander, infinitely more complex tree. The Weavers had orchestrated wars, fostered technological advancements, championed social reforms, and engineered economic downturns, all with an elegant, detached precision. No single individual knew the entirety of the Plan, no leader held absolute authority. Knowledge was passed down through generations via intricate, symbolic transmissions – dreams, carefully chosen texts, and whispered instructions during clandestine gatherings.

Tonight’s initiate was me, Eleanor Vance. I’d spent the last decade as a investigative journalist, specializing in exposing corruption and uncovering hidden power structures. I’d come close, *so close* on several occasions, always pulling back at the last moment, a sudden illness, a lost file, a conveniently timed blackout. My superiors at the *New York Times* had grown increasingly frustrated, my career was stagnating. Then, a cryptic email, a single phrase: “The truth lies beneath the surface,” and an invitation to a dinner party in Florence. That dinner led to a meeting, a interview, and now, this.

The first thing I registered was the smell. Like wet cardboard, decaying fruit, and a faint, persistent undercurrent of lavender. It was a unsettling combination, and profoundly familiar. I’d smelled it before, though I couldn’t quite place when. Or, more accurately, *where*. I was adrift, as I always was, a wisp of regret and lingering memories, perpetually hovering just beyond the veil.

Then I heard it – a rhythmic, dragging thump. *Thump. Thump. Thump.* It was slow, deliberate, and profoundly irritating. I attempted to phase through the wall of a abandoned Victorian parlor, hoping to find a less offensively resonant location, but the sound followed me, clinging to the edges of my spectral awareness. 

Finally, I appeared in the hallway. And there he was.

He was… a mess. Literally. Patches of skin peeled off his face, revealing bone beneath. His clothes were ripped and stained with a disturbing variety of substances. One arm hung uselessly, dangling by a single, blackened tendon. But the most striking thing was his expression. He was staring intensely at a dusty, porcelain doll sitting on a mahogany table.

“You’re… moving,” I stated, the words manifesting as a barely audible shimmer in the air. It was unusual for zombies to exhibit movement beyond the simple, relentless march towards sustenance.

He didn’t react initially. Just continued to stare at the doll, a horrifyingly blank expression on his face. Then, he slowly turned his head, and his gaze landed on me. His eyes, milky white and vacant, widened slightly.

“You’re… floating,” he said, his voice a gravelly, guttural rumble that vibrated through the floorboards. “I thought… I thought I was the only one.”

“I’m worried, Paul; this is the third time you’ve been in my office this week…”

The words hung in the air, subtly weighted with a concern I couldn’t quite place. Director Jenkins’ voice was neutral, professional, a carefully constructed dam against the tide of apprehension I was already feeling. I shifted uncomfortably in the plush, ridiculously uncomfortable chair he’d indicated, the synthetic leather digging into the back of my thighs. My job as a Junior Archivist at the Blackwood Historical Society was, generally, a quiet affair. I spent my days meticulously cataloging documents, preserving photographs, and ensuring the fragile legacy of the Blackwood family was kept safe. Thrills were rare. Confrontations were rarer still.

“Is something the matter, Paul?” he asked, leaning back in his own chair, a gesture that seemed to momentarily destabilize the room’s carefully maintained order. His desk was immaculate, a testament to his obsessive attention to detail – a trait, I was beginning to suspect, he applied to everything.

“Just… a couple of questions about the Smythe collection, sir,” I stammered, immediately regretting the vague response. It felt like burying my head in the sand. “Specifically, regarding the correspondence between Mr. and Mrs. Smythe in 1888.”

The shimmer was the first thing. Just… a ripple in the air, like heat rising off asphalt, but colder. Then the ships arrived. Not the towering, intimidating behemoths we’d imagined, not the black, aggressive shapes from the old Earth military simulations. They were… delicate. Like enormous, iridescent seashells, drifting silently into our skies, casting kaleidoscopic shadows across the world. The Xylos had arrived.

We’d been expecting a war. Centuries of observation, of intercepted signals hinting at a expansionist, utterly ruthless civilization, had led us to brace for annihilation. We’d built bunkers, trained soldiers, stockpiled weapons – largely useless against whatever terrifying technology awaited us. But the Xylos didn’t attack. They simply… established themselves.

Their presence was bewildering. They’d chosen major cities as their initial landing zones – New York, Tokyo, London, São Paulo – and built structures that defied Euclidean geometry. They were made of a material that resembled polished opal, shifting colors with the light, seamlessly blending into the urban landscape. And they were… quiet. No demands, no declarations of dominance, just a pervasive, unsettling stillness.

Then came the announcements. Translated directly into every known language, delivered through a subtle, almost imperceptible, shift in the atmospheric pressure – a kind of sonic vibration – the Xylos communicated their intentions. They were offering “cooperation.” They were offering “assistance.” They were offering to help us manage our… inefficiencies.

That’s when we realized the horrifying truth. The intercepted signals hadn’t shown a technologically superior civilization. They had shown a civilization that had, for centuries, been expanding through brutal conquest, systematically dismantling and absorbing less advanced societies. The Xylos had built their interstellar empire on the ashes of countless worlds, fueled by a terrifyingly simple, yet undeniably effective, strategy: overwhelm and conquer. And they had been doing so with crude weaponry, overwhelming numbers, and sheer, unyielding brutality.

The hum was a constant, a low-frequency thrum woven into the fabric of my existence. It was the sound of the Fortress, my bespoke security system. More accurately, it was the sound of *me* paying for the Fortress. Billion-dollar investments, biometric scanners, laser grids, pressure plates, facial recognition – the whole shebang. I lived in a penthouse apartment atop the Meridian Tower, overlooking the entire city, and I was, objectively, incredibly safe.

Except, I could hear people downstairs.

It had started subtly, a faint rustle of movement, the occasional muffled laugh. Initially, I dismissed it as city noise, the inherent chaos of millions of lives happening beneath my insulated sanctuary. But it persisted, growing incrementally clearer, more… human. At first, I attributed it to a poorly installed soundproofing system, a technician’s oversight during the initial build. I called the company, demanding an investigation. They assured me everything was within specifications, optimized for complete acoustic isolation. “The Fortress is designed to mask all external sounds,” the representative, a relentlessly cheerful man named Dave, had insisted. “You shouldn’t hear anything.”

That was a lie.

Now, six months later, the rustling had solidified into conversations. I could pick out snippets of language – English, mostly, accented with traces of something I couldn’t quite place, maybe a Iberian flair. I knew they were talking *about* me. My name is Barnaby, and I sell potions. Specifically, healing potions. Level 3 healing potions, to be exact. I’ve been selling them for… well, I’ve lost track. Time doesn’t really *exist* in this place anymore, not in the way it used to. It’s just a endless loop of repetitive actions, punctuated by the occasional, utterly predictable event.

Before, there was purpose. Before, there was *players*. Now, there’s just me, the crumbling architecture of the town of Puddlebrook, and the slowly increasing dust that coats everything.

Puddlebrook was… charming, once. A little too charming, perhaps. Every building was meticulously crafted, every cobblestone perfectly placed. The NPCs were voiced with painstaking care, each with a little backstory and a pre-programmed response for every conceivable interaction. I was designed to be the quintessential merchant, perpetually cheerful, always offering a discounted potion to weary adventurers. My lines were: “Greetings, traveler! A weary soul seeks refreshment? A Level 3 healing potion for a mere 50 gold!,” followed by “May your journey be blessed!” – delivered with a genuine (though utterly synthetic) smile.

I haven’t spoken either of those lines in… I think it’s been weeks. Maybe months. The system logs don’t track that anymore. It just says “NPC: Barnaby – Idle.”

It was a fitting aroma for my new existence: a gray, undulating landscape of procedural forests, predictable NPCs, and endless, repetitive quests. I was, technically, “Guardian of the Ancient Grove.” A tutorial enemy.

Ten years. Ten years since the Council, in their infinite, painfully predictable wisdom, had decided my strategic brilliance was “overwhelming” for the new players. They’d “adjusted” my parameters, reduced my threat level, limited my abilities, and banished me to this… this purgatory. Initially, I’d accepted it with a detached, cynical amusement. After all, what was the point of being the Architect of Ruin if no one *ever* felt the weight of my designs? I’d spent my time observing, a silent, obsidian statue in a digital wood, watching waves of eager, naive adventurers stumble through the same predictable loops, their quests culminating in the equally predictable acquisition of a “Shiny Rock.” 

It was… boring. Painfully, existentially boring. 

At first, I’d entertained myself with petty manipulations. A slightly longer loading screen. A particularly aggressive squirrel. A momentary flicker of the sunlight – just to remind them that something, anything, was beyond their control. Simple, insignificant acts of rebellion. But even those had lost their luster. The system, for all its attempts at customization, was ultimately immutable. Every variable was calculated, every outcome predetermined. There was no challenge, no strategic depth, no… *point*.

The air in the Egyptian wing was thick with the ghosts of millennia. Not literal ghosts, of course, though sometimes, standing amongst the towering sarcophagi and painstakingly reconstructed chariots, I half-expected to feel a shiver that had nothing to do with the building’s temperature. It was the weight of history, the sheer, overwhelming volume of lives lived and lost, that pressed down on you. I’d spent countless hours wandering these halls, a habitual tourist of the past, content to observe from a respectful distance, to absorb the grandeur through photographs and whispered audio guides. I’d always been a careful spectator, maintaining a polite, non-intrusive presence. Until today.

I’d been drawn to the collection of canopic jars. Four intricately painted vessels, each representing one of the four sons of Horus – Imsety, Hapy, Duamutef, and Qebehsenuef – tasked with safeguarding the vital organs of the deceased. They were magnificent, polished to a dark sheen despite their age, their vibrant colours remarkably preserved. Each was topped with the head of a different animal: a human-headed Imsety, a baboon-headed Hapy, a jackal-headed Duamutef, and a falcon-headed Qebehsenuef. I’d studied their purpose, their symbolism, the meticulous ritual surrounding their placement in the tomb. I knew everything about them, intellectually, but I hadn't *seen* them. Not truly.

And that’s what had changed. Something had shifted within me, a small, insistent rebellion against the comfortable confines of my detached observation. I was tired of being a passive witness. I was tired of letting the museum dictate the terms of my engagement. I wanted to *feel* it, to connect with these objects on a level beyond comprehension. And suddenly, without conscious thought, I made a decision. I was going to touch one.

The scent was the first thing I remembered. Not of birth, not of mother’s milk, but of lavender and something vaguely metallic – the tang of a forge. I was found, a babe swaddled in coarse wool, in the courtyard of a monastery in 1485, France. The monks, weary of winter and preoccupied with the looming war against England, took me in. They named me Jean, a simple, unremarkable name for a simple, unremarkable child. I was quiet, observant, and possessed an unnerving ability to mimic sounds – the clang of the bell, the murmur of prayers, the scrape of the scribe’s quill.

My childhood was steeped in routine: lessons in Latin, rudimentary farming, and the slow, deliberate pace of monastic life. But as I grew, I began to notice things. Small inconsistencies. A priest who seemed to know too much about the movements of enemy soldiers. A secret chamber tucked behind the refectory. And, most disturbingly, the recurring dream – a vast, shifting landscape of stone, metal, and impossible geometries.

At twenty, I was apprenticed to the monastery’s blacksmith, a gruff, taciturn man named Pierre. He taught me the rhythm of the hammer, the dance of the fire, and the subtle art of shaping metal. But I was restless. The forge felt like a cage, the monastery a prison of the mind. The dreams intensified, growing more vivid, more insistent. I began to draw them – intricate diagrams of interlocking shapes, symbols I couldn’t decipher, fueled by a compulsion I didn’t understand.

Then, the war ended. France was victorious, but the victory was hollow. The monastery was pillaged, the monks slaughtered, and I was left, hidden in the labyrinthine cellars, to survive. I wasn’t particularly fond of the smell, but I’d grown accustomed to it over the decades, a grim perfume marking my work. My name is Elara, and I collect lost children. Specifically, I collect them from those who’d deemed them unworthy of love.

My business was… unconventional. I didn’t offer solace to grieving parents. I offered a alternative. I bought the firstborns.

It had started, like most things of consequence, with a single, desperate plea. A farmer’s wife, face streaked with dirt and tears, had approached me in a shadowed alleyway in a market town. Her husband, a man consumed by drink and despair, had intended to sell her infant son, a wide-eyed little boy named Thomas, to a traveling merchant for a few paltry coins. She’d begged me to intervene, offering everything she had – a few chickens, a worn shawl, and a promise of eternal gratitude. I’d examined the boy, a healthy, robust child with a surprisingly bright laugh. And I’d agreed.

That one act had ignited a purpose. I realized there were countless stories like Thomas’s, whispered in the darkness of villages and towns – children sold to travelling traders, to cruel landowners, to anyone willing to pay a price. The legal system was a tangled mess of corruption and apathy, the authorities often complicit or simply overwhelmed. So I stepped in. I offered a solution. A dark, ethically murky solution, but a solution nonetheless.

The sterile white walls of the International Espionage Academy were, objectively, beautiful. Immaculate. Efficient. Everything a budding operative needed to build a career in shadowy operations, covert surveillance, and, of course, the swift, decisive neutralization of threats. Except, apparently, a appreciation for the finer points of post-kill puns. 

And I was failing. Spectacularly.

I’d mastered extraction techniques – I could liberate a target from a locked vault with a hairpin and a well-placed distraction. My infiltration skills were legendary; I’d once slipped into a fortified Kremlin gala disguised as a catering tray. My proficiency in hand-to-hand combat was, frankly, terrifying. I could dismantle a pressure plate with my bare hands while reciting Shakespeare. I was, in short, a prodigy. Except for Pun-tilation.

Professor Sarcastic, a retired MI6 operative with a permanently raised eyebrow and a penchant for dry wit, had delivered the verdict with the devastating finality of a silenced weapon. “Agent Nightingale,” he’d said, his voice dripping with disdain, “your attempts at post-kill puns are…unacceptable. You’re essentially killing the mission.”

The assignment was simple: after a simulated assassination scenario – a rogue operative designated ‘Subject Zero’ – I had to craft three puns related to the situation. The first was a basic observation, the second a slightly more elaborate play on words, and the third a truly ingenious, darkly humorous conclusion. My first attempt, following the “elimination” of Subject Zero (a remarkably lifelike android programmed to mimic a notorious arms dealer), was “He was a real liability. Now he’s…dealt with.”

Professor Sarcastic had simply stared at me, his eyebrow shooting even higher. “Nightingale, that’s…functional. But a fledgling’s chirping, not a seasoned operative’s commentary.”

The building was a mausoleum of beige. A ten-story, brick behemoth that had stood on the corner of Elm and Oak for as long as I could remember. It was a repository for forgotten businesses, mostly defunct insurance agencies and outdated plumbing supply stores. I’d spent countless afternoons sketching its monotonous facade, trying to capture the weight of its history, the accumulation of decades of dust and disuse. I was an architectural student, obsessed with the stories buildings held, and this one, despite its utter lack of vibrancy, was a particularly compelling subject.

That’s why I was up on the roof, armed with my sketchbook and a increasingly frustrated determination to find *something* interesting. The roof was a depressing plateau of compacted dirt, populated by pigeons and the ghosts of long-gone HVAC units. I’d been sketching the southeast corner, trying to find a angle that would reveal some detail, some crack in the narrative, when I saw it.

A hole.

Not a grand, gaping chasm, but a roughly circular opening in the brickwork, about three feet in diameter, directly in the floor of the third story. It was located in a relatively unassuming area, between a wall of storage and a defunct office space. What was immediately baffling was that it didn’t lead to the floor above. I’d meticulously examined the brickwork surrounding the hole, tracing every seam, every mortar joint. There was no way to access the fourth floor. The walls were solid, the doorways sealed. The hole was simply… there.

My initial reaction was disbelief. A construction error? Some forgotten maintenance job gone awry? But something about the neatness of the cut, the lack of jagged edges, suggested something else entirely. The brick had been cleanly removed, as if a skilled hand had taken a precise bite out of the wall.

In Aethel, eye colour dictated everything. It was law, lineage, destiny. Brown were the farmers, steadfast and rooted to the land, producing the grains that sustained us.
